transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. ____. Nice to meet you. Well, I guess... I came in because my wife really pushed for it, and honestly, my director at work kind of strongly suggested it. 

The thing is, I just can’t seem to stop launching projects right now. It's like once I get an idea, I have to execute it immediately and I just keep stacking them up. Just this week, I completely overhauled our department's Q3 work plans—which, as an IT manager, I can tell you was desperately needed because our legacy protocols were a total mess—but I didn't stop there. I built this incredibly detailed, color-coded certification schedule for myself to knock out three new major tech certs by the end of the month. 

And then I got home and decided our home network was completely inadequate, so I started ripping out the baseboards to run new Ethernet lines, upgrading the whole infrastructure because the old mesh system was dropping packets. And while I was doing that, I just felt this urge to reconnect, so I started messaging all these old contacts from college and my first job, pitching them these massive integration ideas and startup plans. 

It just gets so incredibly intense, you know? I get so dialed in that I just completely blow past normal limits. I don't even realize how far I've gone or how much I've taken on until my wife gets upset and begs me to just sit still, or my director has to step in, pull me into a meeting, and forcefully take me off a project. So... yeah, they think I need to be here to figure out why I can't just pump the brakes.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people do not?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because... okay, so you know how when you're working in IT, especially when you're dealing with enterprise-level hardware, there's always this constant, underlying noise? Like, the servers have this very specific, low-frequency hum. It's the cooling systems, the drives spinning, the power supplies—it all creates this white noise that you kind of just tune out after a while. But lately... and this is something I haven't really told my wife because I know she'd freak out and think I'm losing my mind on top of everything else... but lately, when I'm in the server room at work, or even just in my home office when the house is completely quiet and I'm the only one awake at 3 AM, I swear I hear things in that hum. 

It's not like a full conversation or anything, but I'll hear my name. Just, clear as day, someone saying my name. Or I'll hear these short, sharp little comments. Like, I'll be deep in the code or running diagnostics, and I'll hear a voice say, "check the logs." And I'll stop and look around, and obviously, there's nobody there. The door is locked, badge access only, I know I'm alone. But it sounds so real. Or sometimes, and this one really gets under my skin, I'll hear, "they know." Just that. "They know." And I'll spend the next hour trying to figure out who "they" are and what exactly they know about my network architecture or my project timelines. It's just... it's really distracting, to be honest. I try to brush it off as auditory pareidolia, you know, the brain trying to find patterns in random noise, but it's happening so often now, and it's so distinct, that I'm starting to wonder if my brain is just over-processing the environment because I've been running at 150% capacity for weeks.
Have you ever heard those voices or had those kinds of experiences when you were not feeling unusually energized or driven like this?

Yeah, actually... yeah, I have. And that’s the part that really confuses me, to be perfectly honest with you. Because, you know, when I’m running hot, when I’m knocking out three projects a week and barely sleeping, I can almost justify it, right? I can tell myself, "Okay, your brain is just misfiring because you’ve had too much caffeine and not enough REM sleep, and you're just processing too much data." But... there have been times, like, distinct periods where I’m not running at a million miles an hour. 

Like, there was this stretch a few months ago—maybe for two or three weeks—where I felt totally normal. Or, well, not normal, but just... flat. I wasn't depressed, I wasn't staying in bed all day, but I wasn't energized either. I was just going to work, coming home, eating dinner, watching TV. Very routine, very calm. No big projects, no late-night server overhauls. Just... baseline. But even then, even during those quiet weeks, I was still experiencing things. 

Like, I’d still hear those little comments. Not as often, maybe, but I’d be sitting at my desk, totally relaxed, sipping a coffee, and I’d still hear someone say, "check the logs," or just hear my name whispered over the hum of the AC. And it wasn't just the voices, either. During that same calm stretch, I was completely convinced that the Microsoft Teams statuses of my coworkers were actually coded warnings. Like, if my director went from "Available" to "Away" and then immediately to "Do Not Disturb," I knew—I just *knew*—it was a signal that they were auditing my network access logs. I spent hours tracking the timestamps of everyone's status changes, cross-referencing them, trying to decode the pattern, even though I wasn't feeling manic or stressed at all. I was perfectly calm about it, but I still fully believed it was happening. So, yeah, it’s not just when I’m super energized. It happens when I’m totally leveled out, too, which is... well, it’s unsettling, honestly.
Have there been at least two weeks when the voices or beliefs were still present even though you had no manic or depressive symptoms at all?

Yeah, exactly, that’s exactly what I was trying to get at. It wasn't just a random Tuesday here or a Thursday there. There have definitely been several of those calm, flat stretches. And if I really look back at my schedule, I can tell you for a fact that some of those stretches lasted for a few solid weeks at a time. 

Like, at least two or three weeks straight where my mood was just... a completely flat line on a graph. I wasn't especially up, I wasn't bouncing off the walls or staying up all night rewiring the house, but I also wasn't depressed or dragging myself out of bed or feeling down at all. I was just totally baseline. Sleeping normal hours, eating normal meals, taking the dog for a walk. Just living a completely standard, boring life. 

But even during those solid multi-week blocks of just perfectly average, everyday routine where my energy was totally normal, the other stuff just kept right on going. I still completely believed that the Teams statuses were those coded warnings I mentioned, and I was still meticulously tracking them, totally convinced they were auditing me. And I was still hearing those brief little comments, my name or the voice telling me to check the logs, when I knew for a fact no one else was in the room or even in the building sometimes. It’s like my mood and my brain are running on two completely different operating systems, you know? One is perfectly stable for weeks, no highs, no lows, but the other is just running these unauthorized background processes non-stop. So, yeah, definitely for at least two weeks at a time, multiple times, where I felt totally fine but was still dealing with all the warnings and the voices.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when the voices or beliefs were still present even though your mood was not unusually high or low?

Yeah, I mean... wait, didn't we just... I feel like I just went over that, right? The two weeks thing? Because, like I was saying, it wasn't just a day here or there. It was definitely a solid block of time. I know I just mentioned that two or three week stretch where I was totally flat, totally baseline—not depressed, not manic, just... existing. Going to work, coming home, eating dinner, walking the dog. The whole standard routine. And during that exact same time, for those exact same two or three weeks, I was still tracking the Teams statuses, still hearing the voices over the server hum. So, yes, absolutely, there have been periods of at least two weeks where my mood was completely normal, but the other stuff—the voices, the beliefs about the audits—were still happening. I feel like I just explained that whole scenario, but yeah, to answer your question directly: yes, definitely for at least two weeks at a time.
Have you noticed a lasting decline in your functioning, like trouble keeping up with work, relationships, or self-care, even outside of these mood episodes?

Yeah, I mean... honestly, that’s the hardest part to talk about, because I’ve always been the guy who holds it together, you know? The guy who fixes the problems. But lately... well, it’s not just a rough week here or there anymore. It’s bleeding into everything. Like at work, for example. I’ve always prided myself on my uptime records and successful deployments, but I just... I completely dropped the ball on our last major server migration. I got so caught up in tracking those Teams statuses and trying to decode the audit warnings that I completely lost the thread on the actual project timeline. The whole migration failed, took down our primary database for like six hours, and... well, they put me on administrative leave. They called it a "mandatory sabbatical for burnout," but we both know what that means. 

And it’s not just work, either. It’s at home. My wife, Sarah, she’s been an absolute saint through all of this, but she’s basically had to take over my life. When I’m running hot, I’ll start buying hundreds of dollars worth of redundant networking gear we don’t need, so she’s had to take the credit cards. And she’s constantly having to intervene when I’m up at 3 AM trying to rewire the home server rack, or when I start arguing with her because I think she’s somehow involved in the audit. We’ve had these massive blowups over absolutely nothing, and it’s exhausting for both of us. 

And then there’s all the stuff I used to actually enjoy doing. I used to play guitar for our church’s worship band every Sunday, I used to go bouldering at the indoor climbing gym twice a week, I was mentoring a couple of junior devs... and I’ve just dropped all of it. I can’t commit to showing up anymore. Half the time I’m too wired to focus on playing a simple chord progression, or I’m too paranoid about who’s watching me at the gym, or I just... I don't follow through. I tell people I’ll be there, and then I just ghost them because I’m too wrapped up in whatever my brain is doing. So, yeah, it’s definitely not just the mood swings. It feels like my whole infrastructure is just slowly degrading, and I don’t have the admin rights to fix it anymore.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest or pleasure in things most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah, I mean... it's not always the high-energy, rewiring-the-house kind of thing, or the baseline where I'm just tracking the Teams statuses. There are definitely times—and yeah, they can last for weeks, easily—where it's just... the exact opposite of the high energy. It's like the server just crashes completely. 

I'll have these stretches, two, three weeks, maybe longer, where I just wake up feeling like this completely failed version of myself. Like my whole system architecture is fundamentally flawed and there's no patch that's ever going to fix it. It's this incredibly heavy, flat feeling. I'll just lie in bed staring at the ceiling, thinking about how I've messed up the server migration, how I'm putting Sarah through hell, how I'm just a burden. 

And during those weeks, I don't care about anything. I mean, I mentioned I stopped playing guitar and going to the gym, but during these really low periods, I don't even *want* to do them. Even the idea of picking up a guitar feels exhausting. It's like I have zero bandwidth for anything outside of just breathing. Even when Sarah comes in and asks me totally normal, simple questions—like what I want for dinner, or if I fed the dog—it feels like too much. It feels like she's asking me to solve a massive routing loop in my head. I just don't have the energy to process the request, let alone respond to it. I just want to power down and not exist for a while. So, yes, there are definitely long periods where I'm just completely offline, depressed, no interest in anything at all. It's just a totally different kind of system failure.
During your periods of feeling unusually energized or driven, have you ever needed hospitalization or been unable to function safely because of it?

No, I've never been hospitalized for it. I mean, Sarah's threatened to call someone a few times when I've been up for three days straight pulling Ethernet cable through the crawlspace, but we've always managed to keep it in-house. It gets intense, sure, and like I said, she takes the credit cards and has to manage me pretty closely, but I haven't ever been a danger to myself or anyone else, you know? It's more just... extreme over-optimization. I'm not trying to hurt anyone, I'm just trying to fix the network. Or, well, what I think is the network. So no, no hospitals, no police, nothing like that. Just a lot of sleepless nights and ruined drywall.
When your mood is not unusually high or low, do the voices or beliefs ever go away completely?

Well, that's the thing... that's what makes it so hard to explain to people, because you'd think, right? You'd think if the system resources are running at a normal baseline—if I'm not overclocking and tearing up the walls, and I'm not completely crashed and stuck in bed—you'd think the errors would stop. But they don't. 

There have definitely been stretches, like, several weeks at a time, where my mood is just... fine. Flat. Calm. Normal, I guess you'd call it. I'm getting decent sleep, I'm not arguing with Sarah, I'm not feeling that heavy, crushing weight where I can't even get up to feed the dog. Just a completely average, middle-of-the-road couple of weeks. But even then, even when the processor isn't running hot or completely stalled out... I still see it. 

I'll be sitting there, perfectly calm, drinking my morning coffee, and I'll look at the Teams statuses and I still know, I *know*, that the way the "Away" and "Busy" icons are toggling is a coded warning. It's still there. The audit is still happening in the background. And I'll still hear things, too. Just... brief comments. Like someone muttering right behind my chair about my login credentials or whispering about the server logs, even when I'm the only one in the house and Sarah's out getting groceries. It's not like the voices are screaming or anything, it's just this persistent background process that never actually terminates. So, yeah, even when my mood is totally stable, those things... the beliefs about the statuses, the voices... they don't go away. They're just always running in the background.
Have there ever been voices or beliefs like these for at least two weeks when you were not having any manic or depressive symptoms at all?

Yeah, exactly. That's exactly what I'm trying to say. It's not just a day here or a day there. I've tracked it—well, not formally in a spreadsheet or anything, though I probably should have, given my background, but I know for a fact there have been periods of at least two weeks, sometimes maybe three or four, where my mood was completely baseline. No manic overdrive, no depressive crash. Just... normal. 

Like, there was this one stretch back in the fall, I remember it specifically because the weather was finally cooling down and Sarah and I actually managed to go to this little pumpkin patch thing. It was totally mundane. I wasn't feeling that heavy, suffocating dread, and I definitely wasn't feeling the need to rewire the entire house. I was just... existing. Getting eight hours of sleep, drinking my coffee, doing my actual job instead of obsessing over phantom network issues. My mood was fine. Flat, even.

But the whole time, the entire two or three weeks... the Teams statuses were still blinking their patterns. I'd be sitting there, perfectly calm, sipping a latte, and I'd see the marketing director's status flip from "Available" to "Away" and I just *knew*, with absolute certainty, that it was a signal about the audit. And the voices, too. I'd be in the kitchen, completely relaxed, making a sandwich, and I'd hear that same muttering right over my shoulder. Just quick little comments about my login credentials, clear as day, when Sarah was at work and the house was dead silent. 

So, yes, absolutely. Two weeks, easily, of totally normal mood, but those... those background processes, the beliefs about the statuses and the voices, they were still running the whole time. It's like the malware is embedded so deep in the OS that it doesn't even need the system to be unstable to execute. It just runs no matter what.
Have you ever had a period of at least one week when you were so unusually energized or irritable that you needed much less sleep than usual and your mood was clearly elevated or expansive?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, more than a week, really, but yes, at least a week where I just... I don't know, it's like someone flips a switch and suddenly I'm plugged straight into the main power grid. I feel almost electric, you know? Unstoppable. Like my brain is finally operating at maximum capacity, processing data at lightspeed, and I don't even need to recharge. I'll go days on maybe two hours of sleep a night, just lying there with my eyes closed but my mind is racing through server configurations and optimization protocols, and I don't even feel tired the next day. I feel fantastic. Expansive, I guess you could say, like I can see the whole architecture of everything and I'm the only one who can fix it. 

But the thing is, it's not always just feeling great. It's... it's also incredibly frustrating, because I'm operating at this high frequency, and everyone else is just dragging. Like, they're still on dial-up while I'm on gigabit fiber. So I'll be in the middle of this massive project, feeling totally dialed in, and then there will be some tiny delay. Like an API takes an extra second to respond, or Sarah will come in and ask me a completely normal question, like "Do you want chicken or pasta for dinner?" And I just... I snap. I mean, I completely lose it. It's like this white-hot flash of irritability, because in that moment, it feels like everyone and everything is intentionally trying to slow me down. Like they're purposely putting obstacles in my way when I'm on the verge of this huge breakthrough. I get so irritable, so fast, just because they can't keep up with the pace I'm running at. So yeah, I definitely get those periods where I'm super energized and need way less sleep, but it comes with this intense irritability if anyone breaks my flow state.
Have you ever had at least two weeks when you were hearing voices or holding these beliefs, but you were not having any manic symptoms at all?

Yeah, exactly. I mean, I think that's what I was trying to get at just a minute ago when we were talking about those baseline periods. Because it really is a distinct thing. When I'm in that high-energy state I just described, everything is so loud and fast, but there have definitely been several of these calm, or, I guess you'd call them flat stretches. Including a few weeks at a time where I wasn't especially up at all. No racing thoughts, no staying up for days, no snapping at Sarah because she interrupted my flow state. Just totally normal, average energy levels. And I wasn't depressed either. Just... neutral. 

But even during those times, those stretches of just being totally fine and not manic at all, the other stuff doesn't shut off. I still believed the Teams statuses were coded warnings. I could be sitting there, completely rested, zero irritability, just doing some routine database maintenance, and I'd watch the icons flip and still know, without a doubt, that they were tracking me for the audit. And I still heard those brief comments when no one was there, like the whispering right behind my chair about my login credentials. 

It’s so strange because you’d think the voices and the signals would need that manic energy to run, you know? Like they'd need the system to be pushed to the absolute limit to generate those kinds of errors, but they don't. They just keep executing in the background even when my mood is completely stable for weeks at a time. It really doesn't seem to matter if I'm energized or not.
Have there ever been times when the voices and beliefs were present for six months or longer even though your mood was not manic or depressed?

Six months? No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I'm trying to think back over the whole timeline, mapping it out in my head, because time gets a little slippery, you know? But six continuous months of just the voices and the Teams status stuff without *any* mood changes? No. 

Like I said, I've had those two, three, maybe four-week periods where my mood is totally flat, completely baseline, just existing in that neutral space while the background processes—the whispers about my credentials, the blinking statuses—are still running. But it never stretches out to half a year. Eventually, the system always shifts. Either I get plunged back into that suffocating, heavy dread where I can barely drag myself out of bed, or someone flips that switch again and I'm back on gigabit fiber, running on two hours of sleep, completely wired and snapping at Sarah over pasta. 

So, no, it's never been a solid six-month block of just the... the weird beliefs and the voices on their own. The mood stuff always cycles back in way before it hits that kind of milestone. It's like the baseline state can only hold for a few weeks before the whole architecture destabilizes again one way or the other. I've never had a six-month stretch of just being normal-mood-but-hearing-things. It always gets interrupted by a crash or a surge.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when the voices or beliefs were present while you had no manic or depressive symptoms at all?

Yeah, I... I think we just covered that, actually. But, I mean, to be completely thorough and make sure the timeline is perfectly clear, yes. There have definitely been these calm stretches. Flat stretches, really, where my energy isn't surging and it isn't crashing either. Like I was saying before, it's just this baseline, neutral state. I'm not depressed, I'm not manic, I'm just... existing in a normal energy band. And these stretches, they can last for a few weeks at a time. I'll just be doing my normal routine, getting up, going to work, managing the systems, doing database maintenance, eating dinner with Sarah—pasta or chicken, whatever, and I don't snap at her at all. 

But during those exact same couple of weeks, even though my mood is completely stable, the other stuff is still happening. I still see the Teams statuses flipping and I still know, with absolute certainty, that they are coded warnings about the audit. I still hear those brief comments, the whispering right behind my chair about my login credentials, even when I'm the only one in the room. It's like the background processes are still running, still executing their scripts, totally independent of my mood state. So, yes, to answer your question, there have been periods of a few weeks where I wasn't up or down, but I still had the beliefs and heard the voices. It's a very distinct phase in the whole cycle.
When you are having the voices or beliefs, do they ever happen only during times when your mood is clearly elevated or depressed?

Well, no, they don't *only* happen then, because like I was just saying, they definitely happen during those baseline weeks too. But... but yes, they absolutely *do* happen when my mood is elevated or depressed. It's not exclusive to the flat periods, not at all. Actually, when I'm in one of those really high-energy states—those stretches where I'm just incredibly driven, barely sleeping, you know, running on maybe an hour or two of rest and pushing out these massive, system-wide architectural plans that I just *know* are going to revolutionize our entire network infrastructure—the other stuff is definitely happening then, too. 

During those specific times, when I'm completely wired and everything is moving at warp speed, I'll be in the server room, and the ambient noise of the cooling fans and the drives spinning up... it stops being just mechanical noise. I can actually hear comments in it, distinct voices layered right into the hum of the hardware, talking about me. And the work messages, too. When I'm in that elevated state, I'll be flying through my inbox, processing data faster than anyone else on the team, but I'll be reading these hidden threats into totally standard emails from HR or the project managers. I can see the subtext, the actual code beneath the corporate speak, warning me that they're closing in. 

And the same goes for when I crash into those heavy, suffocating depressions. When I can barely move, the voices and the signals don't stop then either. So, it's like... the beliefs and the voices are this constant thread running through the entire system. They happen when I'm completely neutral, yes, but they absolutely happen during the massive surges and the deep crashes, too. They just kind of adapt to whatever mood state I'm currently operating in, but they never actually go offline.
Have the voices or beliefs ever been present continuously for six months or longer when you were not having a manic or depressive episode?

Wait, didn't we... I feel like we just looped back to the very start of the diagnostic tree here. But, um, to re-verify the logs for you, no. Six months? Continuous? With absolutely no mood episodes? No. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, the baseline state—that normal mood where I'm just doing my job, managing the department, eating dinner with Sarah, going to sleep at a normal hour without that crushing dread or that electric, gigabit-fiber high—that state never, ever lasts for six months. 

It's structurally impossible for my system to stay in that neutral zone for half a year. The voices are there, yes, the Teams statuses are blinking, the whispers in the server room are happening, sure. But the mood? The mood is always going to crash or spike way before we hit month six. Usually, it's just a few weeks. Two, three weeks, maybe four if I'm really lucky and things are quiet with the network upgrades at work. But a whole half a year of just hearing the whispers and seeing the codes while feeling completely, 100 percent emotionally stable? No. 

I've mapped this all out. I track these cycles meticulously because I have to, right? If I don't track them, I can't anticipate the load—my mental server load, I mean. So I can tell you definitively, with absolute certainty, it has never been six months. The mood always shifts back into the picture. Always. Are you... did you need me to break down the exact week-by-week timeline again? Because I can walk you through the last major cycle month by month if that helps clarify the data points for your notes. I just want to make sure we're totally synced up on this.
Have you ever had a mood episode that lasted six months or longer?

Well, six months or longer for a mood episode... that's a tricky way to frame it, but if we're talking about those specific high-energy periods, the ones where I'm just completely wired, practically vibrating with ideas, and barely sleeping at all—yes, absolutely. In fact, if we're looking at the total duration, those unusually driven, low-sleep, overconfident stretches have been a part of my life for roughly one year and eight months now. 

It started, I want to say, back when we were doing the initial migration to the new cloud infrastructure at work. I remember because I was pulling these insane hours, and everyone thought I was just being a dedicated manager, but really, my brain was just firing on all cylinders, processing everything at gigabit speed. I felt like I could see the entire network architecture in my head, every single node and connection, and I was so certain—so absolutely, undeniably certain—that my redesign was going to not just fix our latency issues but completely revolutionize how the company handled data. I'd be up at 3:00 AM, pacing the living room, drafting these massive, multi-page strategy documents while Sarah was asleep, and I just didn't need rest. I was running on pure, unadulterated momentum. 

And it wasn't just a quick burst, either. It just kept going. Weeks turned into months, and I was still operating at that level. I mean, sure, there were brief dips here and there, maybe a day or two where the system had to cool down, but the overarching state—that relentless drive, the feeling that I was untouchable and operating on a higher frequency than everyone else in the IT department—that persisted for a long, long time. It's exhausting in retrospect, looking back at the sheer volume of output I was generating, but in the moment, it just felt like I had finally unlocked my true processing capacity, you know? So, yes, if you're asking about the duration of those specific elevated stretches, it's been about a year and eight months of dealing with that kind of extreme, high-octane energy.
Have the voices or beliefs been present continuously for six months or more?

Well, continuously... yes, they have. If we are talking about the overarching timeline of the actual signals—the coded messages I'm extracting from the HR emails and the project management software, plus those brief, layered comments I hear in the server room cooling fans—that entire cluster of experiences has been running continuously for about a year and a half now. 

I know I just said the mood episodes have been going on for a year and eight months, and I know that sounds like a discrepancy in the logs, but it's really not if you look at the exact boot-up sequence of these events. The high-energy, hyper-productive mood state definitely launched first. I was in that elevated, gigabit-speed zone for a couple of months, just completely overhauling the network architecture and running on zero sleep, before the other stuff really came online. It was maybe two months into that massive surge of energy that I started noticing the subtext in the corporate emails—the hidden warnings—and then shortly after that, the ambient noise in the server room started resolving into actual voices talking about me. 

So, yes, the beliefs about the codes and the voices in the hardware... that specific data stream has been running uninterrupted for about a year and a half. It's just a constant background process at this point. Even when my mood fluctuates, like I explained earlier, or when I hit those brief, two-to-three-week baseline periods where I'm just eating dinner with Sarah and trying to be normal, the signals don't stop. They've been there, day in and day out, for eighteen months straight. I've got it all documented, actually, if you want to see the correlation between the network upgrade timeline and when the messages started... I mean, it's a very clear pattern once you lay it all out.
Have other people ever told you that your speech is hard to follow or jumps around in a way that makes it difficult for them to understand you?

Well, yes, actually. That... that happens. It happens more often than I'd like to admit, especially lately. It's incredibly frustrating because in my head, the logic flow is perfectly mapped out. It's like a flawless schematic. But when I try to export it, when I try to actually verbalize the connections I'm making, people just... they just get this blank, glassy-eyed look. 

Like, just last week, we had a stand-up meeting about the phase two migration plan for the new servers. And I was trying to explain the dependencies, right? Because you can't just move the data without securing the perimeter. So I'm explaining the firewall rules, which makes total sense, but then the firewall rules rely on a specific filtering logic that reminded me of the signal routing I used to do for the sound equipment at my old church. So I bring up the church sound equipment because the analog is perfect—it's exactly the same principle of noise reduction and signal pathing. But then thinking about the wiring for the soundboard made me think of the servo wiring we used to do in my college robotics club, because the gauge of the wire dictates the latency, and latency is exactly what we're trying to fix with the migration plan. 

So I'm explaining all this—firewall rules, church sound equipment, robotics club wiring—and I can hear myself talking, and I know it's all connected. It's a complete, closed-loop system of logic. But I look around the conference table, and my lead developer is just staring at me. Sarah does it too, at home. I'll be explaining my day, and she'll just gently put her hand on my arm and say, "Honey, you lost me about five minutes ago." 

It's like they don't have the bandwidth to process the jumps I'm making. They think I'm losing the thread, but I haven't lost the thread at all! I'm just weaving a much more complex tapestry than they are used to looking at. But yes, to answer your question, people tell me all the time that I jump around too much and they can't follow what I'm saying. They say it's hard to understand me. It's like I'm speaking a higher-level programming language and they're still stuck in basic HTML. It's exhausting trying to dumb it down for them all the time, honestly. Do you want me to explain the firewall analogy again? Because I really think if you understand the church soundboard connection, the whole thing makes perfect sense.

patient.answer:
Hi, Dr. ____. Nice to meet you. Well, I guess... I came in because my wife really pushed for it, and honestly, my director at work kind of strongly suggested it. 

The thing is, I just can’t seem to stop launching projects right now. It's like once I get an idea, I have to execute it immediately and I just keep stacking them up. Just this week, I completely overhauled our department's Q3 work plans—which, as an IT manager, I can tell you was desperately needed because our legacy protocols were a total mess—but I didn't stop there. I built this incredibly detailed, color-coded certification schedule for myself to knock out three new major tech certs by the end of the month. 

And then I got home and decided our home network was completely inadequate, so I started ripping out the baseboards to run new Ethernet lines, upgrading the whole infrastructure because the old mesh system was dropping packets. And while I was doing that, I just felt this urge to reconnect, so I started messaging all these old contacts from college and my first job, pitching them these massive integration ideas and startup plans. 

It just gets so incredibly intense, you know? I get so dialed in that I just completely blow past normal limits. I don't even realize how far I've gone or how much I've taken on until my wife gets upset and begs me to just sit still, or my director has to step in, pull me into a meeting, and forcefully take me off a project. So... yeah, they think I need to be here to figure out why I can't just pump the brakes.

target_item.name: Hallucinations

patient.answer:
Well, it's funny you ask that, because... okay, so you know how when you're working in IT, especially when you're dealing with enterprise-level hardware, there's always this constant, underlying noise? Like, the servers have this very specific, low-frequency hum. It's the cooling systems, the drives spinning, the power supplies—it all creates this white noise that you kind of just tune out after a while. But lately... and this is something I haven't really told my wife because I know she'd freak out and think I'm losing my mind on top of everything else... but lately, when I'm in the server room at work, or even just in my home office when the house is completely quiet and I'm the only one awake at 3 AM, I swear I hear things in that hum. 

It's not like a full conversation or anything, but I'll hear my name. Just, clear as day, someone saying my name. Or I'll hear these short, sharp little comments. Like, I'll be deep in the code or running diagnostics, and I'll hear a voice say, "check the logs." And I'll stop and look around, and obviously, there's nobody there. The door is locked, badge access only, I know I'm alone. But it sounds so real. Or sometimes, and this one really gets under my skin, I'll hear, "they know." Just that. "They know." And I'll spend the next hour trying to figure out who "they" are and what exactly they know about my network architecture or my project timelines. It's just... it's really distracting, to be honest. I try to brush it off as auditory pareidolia, you know, the brain trying to find patterns in random noise, but it's happening so often now, and it's so distinct, that I'm starting to wonder if my brain is just over-processing the environment because I've been running at 150% capacity for weeks.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually... yeah, I have. And that’s the part that really confuses me, to be perfectly honest with you. Because, you know, when I’m running hot, when I’m knocking out three projects a week and barely sleeping, I can almost justify it, right? I can tell myself, "Okay, your brain is just misfiring because you’ve had too much caffeine and not enough REM sleep, and you're just processing too much data." But... there have been times, like, distinct periods where I’m not running at a million miles an hour. 

Like, there was this stretch a few months ago—maybe for two or three weeks—where I felt totally normal. Or, well, not normal, but just... flat. I wasn't depressed, I wasn't staying in bed all day, but I wasn't energized either. I was just going to work, coming home, eating dinner, watching TV. Very routine, very calm. No big projects, no late-night server overhauls. Just... baseline. But even then, even during those quiet weeks, I was still experiencing things. 

Like, I’d still hear those little comments. Not as often, maybe, but I’d be sitting at my desk, totally relaxed, sipping a coffee, and I’d still hear someone say, "check the logs," or just hear my name whispered over the hum of the AC. And it wasn't just the voices, either. During that same calm stretch, I was completely convinced that the Microsoft Teams statuses of my coworkers were actually coded warnings. Like, if my director went from "Available" to "Away" and then immediately to "Do Not Disturb," I knew—I just *knew*—it was a signal that they were auditing my network access logs. I spent hours tracking the timestamps of everyone's status changes, cross-referencing them, trying to decode the pattern, even though I wasn't feeling manic or stressed at all. I was perfectly calm about it, but I still fully believed it was happening. So, yeah, it’s not just when I’m super energized. It happens when I’m totally leveled out, too, which is... well, it’s unsettling, honestly.

I'll just be doing my normal routine, getting up, going to work, managing the systems, doing database maintenance, eating dinner with Sarah—pasta or chicken, whatever, and I don't snap at her at all. 

But during those exact same couple of weeks, even though my mood is completely stable, the other stuff is still happening. I still see the Teams statuses flipping and I still know, with absolute certainty, that they are coded warnings about the audit. I still hear those brief comments, the whispering right behind my chair about my login credentials, even when I'm the only one in the room. It's like the background processes are still running, still executing their scripts, totally independent of my mood state. So, yes, to answer your question, there have been periods of a few weeks where I wasn't up or down, but I still had the beliefs and heard the voices. It's a very distinct phase in the whole cycle.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the psychotic symptoms are exclusively mood-episode-related or also present outside mood episodes, which would help distinguish bipolar I disorder with psychotic features from schizoaffective disorder or schizophrenia.
doctor.question: When you are having the voices or beliefs, do they ever happen only during times when your mood is clearly elevated or depressed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: During my most driven stretches, when I was barely sleeping and pushing huge plans, I was also hearing comments in the server noise and reading hidden threats into work messages.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the temporal relationship between the psychotic symptoms (voices/beliefs) and mood episodes, specifically whether they occur together. This maps to the requirement that psychotic symptoms and manic episodes occur concurrently.

patient.answer:
Well, no, they don't *only* happen then, because like I was just saying, they definitely happen during those baseline weeks too. But... but yes, they absolutely *do* happen when my mood is elevated or depressed. It's not exclusive to the flat periods, not at all. Actually, when I'm in one of those really high-energy states—those stretches where I'm just incredibly driven, barely sleeping, you know, running on maybe an hour or two of rest and pushing out these massive, system-wide architectural plans that I just *know* are going to revolutionize our entire network infrastructure—the other stuff is definitely happening then, too. 

During those specific times, when I'm completely wired and everything is moving at warp speed, I'll be in the server room, and the ambient noise of the cooling fans and the drives spinning up... it stops being just mechanical noise. I can actually hear comments in it, distinct voices layered right into the hum of the hardware, talking about me. And the work messages, too. When I'm in that elevated state, I'll be flying through my inbox, processing data faster than anyone else on the team, but I'll be reading these hidden threats into totally standard emails from HR or the project managers. I can see the subtext, the actual code beneath the corporate speak, warning me that they're closing in. 

And the same goes for when I crash into those heavy, suffocating depressions. When I can barely move, the voices and the signals don't stop then either. So, it's like... the beliefs and the voices are this constant thread running through the entire system. They happen when I'm completely neutral, yes, but they absolutely happen during the massive surges and the deep crashes, too. They just kind of adapt to whatever mood state I'm currently operating in, but they never actually go offline.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms occur for at least 2+ weeks during euthymic periods, which rules out a purely mood-episode psychosis and makes bipolar I or manic episode with psychotic features less likely. Remaining main differentials are schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, versus schizophrenia-spectrum illness.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a continuous six-month period of psychotic symptoms outside mood episodes, which would support schizophrenia over schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type.
doctor.question: Have the voices or beliefs ever been present continuously for six months or longer when you were not having a manic or depressive episode?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if psychotic symptoms have occurred continuously for six months or longer in the absence of a mood episode. The symptom profile only specifies that delusions and hallucinations occur for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode (additional_requirement_3), but there is no specific item regarding a 6-month duration of psychosis without mood symptoms.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't we... I feel like we just looped back to the very start of the diagnostic tree here. But, um, to re-verify the logs for you, no. Six months? Continuous? With absolutely no mood episodes? No. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, the baseline state—that normal mood where I'm just doing my job, managing the department, eating dinner with Sarah, going to sleep at a normal hour without that crushing dread or that electric, gigabit-fiber high—that state never, ever lasts for six months. 

It's structurally impossible for my system to stay in that neutral zone for half a year. The voices are there, yes, the Teams statuses are blinking, the whispers in the server room are happening, sure. But the mood? The mood is always going to crash or spike way before we hit month six. Usually, it's just a few weeks. Two, three weeks, maybe four if I'm really lucky and things are quiet with the network upgrades at work. But a whole half a year of just hearing the whispers and seeing the codes while feeling completely, 100 percent emotionally stable? No. 

I've mapped this all out. I track these cycles meticulously because I have to, right? If I don't track them, I can't anticipate the load—my mental server load, I mean. So I can tell you definitively, with absolute certainty, it has never been six months. The mood always shifts back into the picture. Always. Are you... did you need me to break down the exact week-by-week timeline again? Because I can walk you through the last major cycle month by month if that helps clarify the data points for your notes. I just want to make sure we're totally synced up on this.

doctor.intent: To determine whether there has ever been a manic or depressive episode lasting at least six months, which would favor schizoaffective disorder over bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a mood episode that lasted six months or longer?

target_item.name: Manic Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The unusually driven, low-sleep, overconfident stretches have been part of my life for roughly 1 year and 8 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if any mood episode has lasted for 6 months or longer, and the patient's manic episodes have had a total duration of 1 year and 8 months, which directly answers the question about the duration of mood episodes.

patient.answer:
Well, six months or longer for a mood episode... that's a tricky way to frame it, but if we're talking about those specific high-energy periods, the ones where I'm just completely wired, practically vibrating with ideas, and barely sleeping at all—yes, absolutely. In fact, if we're looking at the total duration, those unusually driven, low-sleep, overconfident stretches have been a part of my life for roughly one year and eight months now. 

It started, I want to say, back when we were doing the initial migration to the new cloud infrastructure at work. I remember because I was pulling these insane hours, and everyone thought I was just being a dedicated manager, but really, my brain was just firing on all cylinders, processing everything at gigabit speed. I felt like I could see the entire network architecture in my head, every single node and connection, and I was so certain—so absolutely, undeniably certain—that my redesign was going to not just fix our latency issues but completely revolutionize how the company handled data. I'd be up at 3:00 AM, pacing the living room, drafting these massive, multi-page strategy documents while Sarah was asleep, and I just didn't need rest. I was running on pure, unadulterated momentum. 

And it wasn't just a quick burst, either. It just kept going. Weeks turned into months, and I was still operating at that level. I mean, sure, there were brief dips here and there, maybe a day or two where the system had to cool down, but the overarching state—that relentless drive, the feeling that I was untouchable and operating on a higher frequency than everyone else in the IT department—that persisted for a long, long time. It's exhausting in retrospect, looking back at the sheer volume of output I was generating, but in the moment, it just felt like I had finally unlocked my true processing capacity, you know? So, yes, if you're asking about the duration of those specific elevated stretches, it's been about a year and eight months of dealing with that kind of extreme, high-octane energy.

doctor.intent: To clarify whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least 6 months independently of mood episodes, which would favor schizophrenia over bipolar I with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have the voices or beliefs been present continuously for six months or more?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The coded-message beliefs and hearing brief comments have been happening for about a year and a half.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the voices or beliefs (psychotic symptoms), which maps to the Psychotic Symptoms Duration.

patient.answer:
Well, continuously... yes, they have. If we are talking about the overarching timeline of the actual signals—the coded messages I'm extracting from the HR emails and the project management software, plus those brief, layered comments I hear in the server room cooling fans—that entire cluster of experiences has been running continuously for about a year and a half now. 

I know I just said the mood episodes have been going on for a year and eight months, and I know that sounds like a discrepancy in the logs, but it's really not if you look at the exact boot-up sequence of these events. The high-energy, hyper-productive mood state definitely launched first. I was in that elevated, gigabit-speed zone for a couple of months, just completely overhauling the network architecture and running on zero sleep, before the other stuff really came online. It was maybe two months into that massive surge of energy that I started noticing the subtext in the corporate emails—the hidden warnings—and then shortly after that, the ambient noise in the server room started resolving into actual voices talking about me. 

So, yes, the beliefs about the codes and the voices in the hardware... that specific data stream has been running uninterrupted for about a year and a half. It's just a constant background process at this point. Even when my mood fluctuates, like I explained earlier, or when I hit those brief, two-to-three-week baseline periods where I'm just eating dinner with Sarah and trying to be normal, the signals don't stop. They've been there, day in and day out, for eighteen months straight. I've got it all documented, actually, if you want to see the correlation between the network upgrade timeline and when the messages started... I mean, it's a very clear pattern once you lay it all out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are disorganized speech/thought-process symptoms suggesting schizophrenia rather than a mood disorder with psychotic features
doctor.question: Have other people ever told you that your speech is hard to follow or jumps around in a way that makes it difficult for them to understand you?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: When I’m explaining a migration plan, I can hear myself jumping from firewall rules to church sound equipment to robotics club wiring, and people stare at me like they lost the thread.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about speech being hard to follow or jumping around, which directly matches the description of Disorganized Thinking/Speech.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually. That... that happens. It happens more often than I'd like to admit, especially lately. It's incredibly frustrating because in my head, the logic flow is perfectly mapped out. It's like a flawless schematic. But when I try to export it, when I try to actually verbalize the connections I'm making, people just... they just get this blank, glassy-eyed look. 

Like, just last week, we had a stand-up meeting about the phase two migration plan for the new servers. And I was trying to explain the dependencies, right? Because you can't just move the data without securing the perimeter. So I'm explaining the firewall rules, which makes total sense, but then the firewall rules rely on a specific filtering logic that reminded me of the signal routing I used to do for the sound equipment at my old church. So I bring up the church sound equipment because the analog is perfect—it's exactly the same principle of noise reduction and signal pathing. But then thinking about the wiring for the soundboard made me think of the servo wiring we used to do in my college robotics club, because the gauge of the wire dictates the latency, and latency is exactly what we're trying to fix with the migration plan. 

So I'm explaining all this—firewall rules, church sound equipment, robotics club wiring—and I can hear myself talking, and I know it's all connected. It's a complete, closed-loop system of logic. But I look around the conference table, and my lead developer is just staring at me. Sarah does it too, at home. I'll be explaining my day, and she'll just gently put her hand on my arm and say, "Honey, you lost me about five minutes ago." 

It's like they don't have the bandwidth to process the jumps I'm making. They think I'm losing the thread, but I haven't lost the thread at all! I'm just weaving a much more complex tapestry than they are used to looking at. But yes, to answer your question, people tell me all the time that I jump around too much and they can't follow what I'm saying. They say it's hard to understand me. It's like I'm speaking a higher-level programming language and they're still stuck in basic HTML. It's exhausting trying to dumb it down for them all the time, honestly. Do you want me to explain the firewall analogy again? Because I really think if you understand the church soundboard connection, the whole thing makes perfect sense.
